title: 5 V supply, red LED drops about 2 V, you want 20 mA. Which resistor do you pick?
explain: The resistor takes the rest of the voltage: 5 V - 2 V = 3 V. R = V / I = 3 / 0.02 = 150 Ω. 330 Ω also works but gives only about 9 mA, so the LED is dim. 100 Ω gives 30 mA, which is too much for most small LEDs.

title: Three 1.5 V batteries in series, then one 150 Ω resistor to the other end. What current flows?
explain: Voltages add in series: 3 x 1.5 V = 4.5 V. I = V / R = 4.5 / 150 = 0.03 A = 30 mA. Putting batteries in parallel would keep 1.5 V and only add capacity.

title: Servo angle to ticks. On the Uno unsigned int is 16-bit (uint16_t here). angle = 45. What does this print?
explain: 45 * 2000 = 90000 does not fit in 16 bits. It wraps to 90000 - 65536 = 24464. Then 24464 / 180 = 135, so you get 2135, not 2500. Use unsigned long (32-bit) for the multiplication.

title: Servo on Timer1, Fast PWM mode 14 (TOP = ICR1). 16 MHz clock, prescaler 8, signal 50 Hz. Which ICR1 value do you write?
explain: Timer clock = 16 MHz / 8 = 2 MHz. One period of 20 ms is 2,000,000 / 50 = 40000 ticks. The timer counts from 0 to TOP, which is TOP + 1 steps. So TOP = 39999.

title: MODER starts as 0xFFFFFFFF. GPIO_Init clears the 2 bits of pin 5, then sets mode 1 (output). What is MODER now?
explain: Pin 5 uses bits 11:10, so the shift is 2 * 5 = 10. The clear mask 3 << 10 = 0xC00 gives 0xFFFFF3FF. Then OR with 1 << 10 = 0x400 gives 0xFFFFF7FF. Without the clear step, old bits stay set.

title: After reset, some static variables are not zero. Tap the bug.
explain: Pointer subtraction on uint32_t * gives a count of words, not bytes. memset gets a size four times too small, so only the first quarter of .bss is cleared. Cast both pointers to uint8_t * (or multiply by 4).

title: Interrupts on the Uno: 5 rules before lesson 8
bullets: Keep the ISR short. Set a flag or save a value, then return. Do the real work in loop().
A variable shared with an ISR must be volatile, or the compiler may keep an old copy in a register.
A 16-bit value is read in two steps on an 8-bit AVR. Turn interrupts off for a moment while you copy it, or you can read half old and half new data.
delay() does not work inside an ISR, and millis() does not move there. Serial.print can block when its buffer is full.
Buttons bounce. An interrupt on every edge fires many times, so you still need debounce.

title: An ISR sets bool pressed = true; and loop() runs while (!pressed) {}. With -O2 the program hangs forever. Why, and what fixes it?
options: The compiler assumes nothing else changes pressed. Declare it volatile.
The ISR is too long. Make it shorter.
bool is 16-bit on AVR, so the write is lost.
explain: The loop never writes pressed, so the optimizer reads it once and loops on a register copy. volatile forces a real read each time. For a one-byte flag this is enough. For a multi-byte value you also need atomic access.

title: A 7805 gets 9 V from a battery and feeds a 100 mA load at 5 V. How much power turns into heat in the regulator?
explain: A linear regulator drops the extra voltage and burns it. P = (Vin - Vout) x I = (9 - 5) x 0.1 = 0.4 W. The load gets 0.5 W. The regulator wastes almost as much as it delivers, so a battery runs out fast.

title: pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP). The button connects pin 2 to GND. What does digitalRead(2) return while the button is pressed?
options: It floats, so it is random
LOW only after a debounce delay
explain: The internal pull-up (about 20 to 50 kΩ) holds the pin HIGH when the button is open. Pressing it connects the pin to GND, so it reads LOW. The logic is inverted: pressed = LOW.
